summary: Three fixes to shipped behaviour, all verified by driving the real screens rather than by unit tests. (1) A face-recognition alert now says WHO. The recognized identity lived only in alert.Label, which the notification body prints only when a destination's 'label' field is enabled - with it off, a match delivered 'Lobby Entrance - 94% confidence' and named nobody. The structured Data map that webhook/MQTT/Telegram/email consumers actually read never carried the identity at all, on any destination. apps/mymatasan/services/notification.go's renderVisionAlert now adds a person line to the body when the label is suppressed and always promotes person/personId/recognized/faceConfidence into Data; recognized:false is always sent so a consumer can route on strangers, and an unrecognized face is never given a name. alertTemplateContext gained the {{person}}, {{recognized}} and {{faceConfidence}} custom-field tokens - {{person}} was DOCUMENTED in infra/vision/object.go and never implemented, so every custom field using it silently expanded to nothing. (2) The in-app Notifications page showed neither the person nor the plate. Its AI row never renders the notification body; it builds its own field list, and 'objectLabel' there is the RAW worker label, which deliberately wins over alert.Label - so a recognized person rendered as 'Object: face' and a read plate as 'Object: license plate'. notifications.js now reads the identity the detector promotes into the alert's metadata and shows Person (face) and Plate (LPR). On a face alert the generic Confidence is replaced by a Match score: the stored alert confidence is max(matchScore, 0.5), so it was a floored duplicate on a recognized face and a hard-coded 50% presented as measured on an unrecognized one. A stranger is labelled 'Unknown person' rather than omitted. Four notif.* keys added across en/ms/zh/ar. (3) Refreshing the page threw the operator back to the dashboard in mymatasan, myseliasan, myiotsan and mypintusan. New frontend/shared/src/stickyTab.js (useStickyTab/read/write/clearStickyTab) remembers the active section in sessionStorage - per tab, never sent to the server, and it survives reload and restore-after-crash. It takes the set of sections the signed-in user may reach, so a section that was renamed by an upgrade, or one an administrator left behind before a viewer signed in on the same tab, falls back to the landing page and the stale value is rewritten rather than bouncing again; sign-out forgets the section so the next person does not land inside the last operator's work. In mymatasan the actual culprit was separate: enterApp forced the dashboard on entry and the session-restore path ran through it, so even a section every role can reach did not survive - it now takes a keepSection option that a refresh sets and a fresh sign-in does not.
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no schema, config, API-route or restart change. Notification payloads only GAIN fields: person/personId/recognized/faceConfidence appear on face alerts and nothing existing was renamed or removed, so an existing webhook, MQTT subscriber or Telegram destination keeps working untouched and simply starts receiving the identity. A destination with the 'label' field enabled sees no new person line in the body (the label already carries the name); one with it disabled gains a line where it previously had none. The three new template tokens resolve to empty on non-face alerts, matching how the existing plate tokens behave, so a custom field that already used {{person}} starts resolving instead of silently expanding to nothing. On the Notifications screen the generic Confidence row disappears from FACE alerts only and is replaced by Match; plate and every other alert type are unchanged. The remembered section is per browser tab and is cleared on sign-out, so nothing is persisted across users or shared between tabs; a browser that blocks storage simply does not remember the section rather than failing to load. myidsan is deliberately NOT changed - it already remembered its active section through its own cookie and shows an explicit unauthorized page rather than a silent demotion, which is the better behaviour of the two; unifying them would be a behaviour change for its users, not a fix.
